title: Half-empty locker
passages:
The flat bar bit into the cam at the locker's lower hinge. Miko didn't ask permission; she'd stopped asking three nodes back. The steel shrieked, a sound that pulled heads from the parts bins and the bench grinder alike. Nour didn't flinch. She stood with her arms folded, one boot braced on the drawer unit, watching the bar leverage the latch free.

"Sixty-three seals short of a full card," Nour said. Her voice carried over the grind of the bar. "You pop that, the log writes your badge to the latch and nothing else. Five minutes of shift overlap, key on the yard hook, and half the stock walks. You want that on your ticket, Miko?"

Miko grunted, shoulders driving the bar down. The cam gave with a crack. "I want to know who took them. The log swears nobody came. So either the log lies or somebody walked through the wall."

The door swung wide. Sixty-one lead-and-wire seals hung on pins stamped for a hundred twenty-four. Each seal bore a stamped number, each number written neat on the tally card clipped to the door's inner face. The pins caught the shop light, dull gray rows with gaps like missing teeth.

Nour stepped closer, close enough to smell the grease on Miko's sleeve. "Sixty-one. That's what the inventory reads. That's what the board will read when the shift-change audit hits. You just made the shortage public, loader. Congratulations."

A folded dispatch line sat in the door slot, creased sharp from the down-line run. Kettering header, Bay 4 routing, Shift 2 consignment block. Teodoro peeled it out without looking at either of them. His eyes tracked the seal numbers on the paper, then the pins, then back to the paper. He reached for the pod's plate on the bench beside Ivo's cartridge.

Teodoro lifted the pod's plate from the bench. The metal tag was warm from the bench lamp, its etched numbers sharp under the light. He held it beside the dispatch line, eyes moving line by line.

"K-7741," he read. "K-7742. K-7743. K-7744. K-7745." His finger tracked down the paper. "K-7741. K-7742. K-7743. K-7744. K-7745."

He set the plate down. The *clack* was small in the shop's hum.

"Every number on that lid came off these pins," Teodoro said. He didn't look at Nour. "Anza stock. Anza shift. Somebody walked them out the door and crimped a man into a medical pod with our own seals."

Marlowe shifted on the couch. His good hand braced the cushions; the other arm lay immobilized against his chest, the splint Teodoro had fashioned from a loader's splint kit and a length of PVC pipe. His face was pale, a scrape along the jaw darkening to bruise.

"Anza's hospitality has improved since the last time," Marlowe said. His voice was rough, the sedative still dragging at the edges. "Last time they just left me at the siding with a ration bar and a radio that didn't work."

Nour's hand closed over the tally card before Miko could pull it back. The clipboard didn't tear; Miko let it go with a sharp exhale. Nour flipped to the back page, the consignment block. Her own initials sat at the bottom of the column, neat and small: *N. Varel, Sr. Loader, Shift 1*.

She read the numbers above her signature. Bay 4. Shift 2. Four rigs. Seal ranges she'd authorized with a pen stroke and a glance at the manifest.

"Senior signs every consignment," she said. The words came flat, like she was reading a spec sheet. "I never counted what I was signing."

The shop noise didn't stop. The bench grinder kept whining. A loader's radio crackled somewhere in the bay. But the space around the locker went quiet.

Miko's flat bar hung loose in her grip. "You signed thirty-four seals out of Bay 4 last cycle," she said. "Twenty-nine the cycle before. You didn't notice the pins were light?"

Nour's thumb traced the edge of the card. "I noticed the roster stayed full. I noticed resupply came through on time. I noticed the node ate through winter." She looked up, eyes dry. "That's what I noticed."

Teodoro picked up the dispatch line again. He folded it slow, creases lining up. "The line's forger has been pulling from our stock. That means somebody here handed them over. Somebody with access to the yard hook during overlap."

"Or somebody who knew the key hung there," Miko said. "Which is everybody who's ever worked a shift change."

Ivo's cartridge ticked on the bench. 00:63:18. The numbers dropped steady, indifferent.

Rhea stood at the plate, her condition entry still glowing PENDING COUNTERSIGN. She hadn't moved since Teodoro set the pod's tag down. Her wrench rested on the bench beside the respirator parts, forgotten.

"Sixty-one seals left," Rhea said. "Sixty-three short. That's four rigs' worth, minimum. Four rigs that got crimped with Anza numbers and sent down-line clean."

"Four ghost rigs," Teodoro said. "Kass tracked four at Kettering. One vanished at 04:51."

Nour's fingers tightened on the clipboard. The card didn't leave her grip. Her initials *N. Varel* stared up under the shop lights, ink she'd laid down herself, authorizing seals she'd never touched.

Nour turned, the clipboard held against her ribs like a shield. Her boots didn't hurry. They didn't need to.

"Arithmetic," she said to the shop at large. "Signed shortage on the tally card. Frozen warrant on the board. A medical rig with its transponder cut out sitting dead at the ore siding, and a man breathing on the couch who was logged as four-twelve kilos of ballast. That flags Anza contested. Thin roster through winter. Resupply delayed. Shifts unfilled. Pell takes the box and the paper, he closes his claim, he goes home satisfied. The node survives."

She passed the bench. Ivo's cartridge ticked: 00:63:12. Rhea didn't look up from the plate.

"The card is why running fails too," Rhea said. Her voice was low, stripped of its usual edge. "You hand him over with the shortage attached, the line reads the shortage as conspiracy. Anza becomes the node that fed the forger. Every rig we touch gets audited. Every loader gets watched. We don't just lose resupply. We lose the line."

"Then we run," Miko said. She hadn't moved from the locker. The flat bar rested across her palm, forgotten. "Marlowe walks out under one of my tickets. I know a coast runner who owes me a blind berth. We're gone before the audit lands."

Nour stopped at the door. Her hand found the clipboard's edge, fingers brushing her own initials. *N. Varel, Sr. Loader, Shift 1*.

"You're doing sums with Ivo's air," Miko said. The words landed flat. "Every minute you argue, that cartridge drops. He has fifty-two minutes left. Maybe less if the patch fails. You want to trade a man for a roster spot? Fine. But don't call it arithmetic. Call it what it is."

Nour's jaw tightened. The shop held its breath. The bench grinder whined. Somewhere a radio squelched static.

"Fifty-two minutes," Nour repeated. She didn't turn. "Pell's at the north gate at oh-six-hundred with a second signature. That's eighteen minutes. He takes the pod, the warrant lifts, the board unfreezes. Resupply moves. The node eats."

She pocketed the tally card. The clipboard followed, tucked under her arm.

"Eighteen minutes," she said. "I'll walk the ballast to his cradle myself."

The door swung shut behind her.
